Sources indicate that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Initiative, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

Recent findings suggest that what took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable proposal, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped challenges, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that strategy into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

It has been revealed that writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

It has been revealed that after spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

It has been revealed that smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard demonstrates intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up complications, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

In a recent development, take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count notes you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”.

What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

📅 13 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim.
  • In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.
  • It has been revealed that questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯.

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

It has been revealed that questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:.

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully.".

In a recent development, note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

What has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:.

In a recent development, participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants rolled out 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:.

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:.

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:.

51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:.

35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:.

It has been revealed that the paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

Recent findings suggest that A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Sources indicate that theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

An evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

According to recent reports, 🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

We have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:.

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a newly introduced arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗.

The most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:.

According to recent reports, pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

It has been revealed that some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics mentioned "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check.".

So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

To the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

Recent findings suggest that stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗.

It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

I have been working on a complementary experiment at https://ReproducibleAIList.org, though not the same scale. We've been taking models from Chip Huyen's GoodAIList.com and having a clean-room agent try to reproduce each one from scratch using the code repos (not the papers).

One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.

Very cool, roar sounds like a great package! I'll take a look and see what we can learn from roar.

Really enjoyed being part of this experiment. Gratifying to see our reproduction highlighted as one of the community’s best.

“A Coin Flip for Safety” was reproduced using AlphaXiv’s OpenResearch with OpenCode’s free BigPickle model, with experiments run locally on 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090s.

It was a great demonstration of how agent-assisted research can make independent reproduction and auditing accessible with relatively modest compute.

Thanks to the Hugging Face and AlphaXiv teams for organizing the challenge and making the whole process open and reproducible!

Really enjoyed being part of this experiment. Gratifying to see our reproduction highlighted as one of the community’s best.“A Coin Flip for Safety” was reproduced using AlphaXiv’s OpenResearch with OpenCode’s free BigPickle model, with experiments run locally on 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090s.It was a great demonstration of how agent-assisted research can make independent reproduction and auditing accessible with relatively modest compute.Thanks to the Hugging Face and AlphaXiv teams for organizing the challenge and making the whole process open and reproducible!One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us bilibili the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

The scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days demonstrates how quickly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻.

Industry observers note that what I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊.

The point about reviewing capacity is particularly important... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️.

Recent findings suggest that most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inception, a upcoming data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise.

In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a fresh group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.”.

The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name.

Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests.

According to recent reports, inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement claims. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”.

Sources indicate that the gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote.

Industry observers note that plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.”.

Industry observers note that “Inception is a fresh group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.”.

To be fair, the latest crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters.

That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs.

And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation.

Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility.

Inception, for its part, indicates it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®.

Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.
  • Industry observers note that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Sources indicate that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

Industry observers note that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every upcoming checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

Sources indicate that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Sources indicate that where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

When the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:.

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

Recent findings suggest that strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:.

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

It has been revealed that each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:.

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Sources indicate that now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Recent findings suggest that buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise plans billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

Recent findings suggest that how much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a newly introduced file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

According to recent reports, figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

To train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":.

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

According to recent reports, nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:.

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

In a recent development, if you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of fresh code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:.

Recent findings suggest that buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:.

Industry observers note that A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise plans, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions announced as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

In a recent development, nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

It has been revealed that if your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

The full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

Industry observers note that run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

It has been revealed that prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's proposal before anything moves.

According to recent reports, training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Sources indicate that bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Industry observers note that only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

The loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:.

Recent findings suggest that stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Industry observers note that contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an concern with what worked and what didn't.

According to recent reports, what makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.
  • A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.
  • According to recent reports, this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.

A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

According to recent reports, this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of Latest York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision says Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors highlighted evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”.

Another item of evidence apparently revealed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”.

Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ notes.

The feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”.

Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”.

“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.

Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Recent findings suggest that washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese organization return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®.

Latest Update: GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • Sources indicate that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

Sources indicate that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

Industry observers note that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Industry observers note that reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in customers. More details on these and other incidents follow.

Recent findings suggest that the East US 3 buildout is about one week behind initiative. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to upgrade, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Recent findings suggest that actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

Industry observers note that A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

Sources indicate that the importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Sources indicate that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

In a recent development, web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

It has been revealed that during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Sources indicate that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

According to recent reports, some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, newly introduced connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

In a recent development, we took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the problem.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

In a recent development, copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Problems, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

Sources indicate that A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

According to recent reports, the pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

#115430. State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

📅 14 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2744 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in the AI world, time feels compressed.
  • It has been revealed that models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis.
  • There used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

It has been revealed that models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

There used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

The chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

Two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

That leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

Sources indicate that the two organizations publishing the most latest open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

According to recent reports, when smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

In a recent development, more hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

At the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

According to recent reports, AMD contributed many conversions. This work is notable: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

Industry observers note that we took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

We counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

In a recent development, the two numbers record different acts. A like notes a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it presently depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

According to recent reports, china's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

The difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, demonstrates the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Time also plays an notable role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

Sources indicate that if frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below reveals a different story.

Of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses.

DeepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

Sources indicate that whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

Qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 fresh repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual debuts. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

Sources indicate that these factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future people.

This position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

According to recent reports, among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

So how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

In February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most vital project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

The ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

And that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

Industry observers note that model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

According to recent reports, across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

In a recent development, we could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

In a recent development, claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

It has been revealed that the second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen new client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

Industry observers note that we spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

It has been revealed that then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

Compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

However, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the big models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future users. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

The metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

Government may apply TV license fee to streaming services to fund the BBC
