💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • Recent findings suggest that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

Recent findings suggest that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many latest tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Recent findings suggest that feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

In a recent development, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

In a recent development, consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

Industry observers note that these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

It has been revealed that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

According to recent reports, autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into latest executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

In a recent development, autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

According to recent reports, we distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

Recent findings suggest that the generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Recent findings suggest that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a latest target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

It has been revealed that the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

Industry observers note that to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

In a recent development, together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Sources indicate that generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Industry observers note that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Recent findings suggest that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Recent findings suggest that failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

Sources indicate that A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

Sources indicate that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Recent findings suggest that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We blueprint to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

According to recent reports, autoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

Sources indicate that the training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Recent findings suggest that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The IndiaAI Mission revealed on November 25, 2026, that Ministry of Electronics and IT Secretary S. Krishnan had inaugurated Chariot Artificial Intelligence’s Chariot-1 foundation models, developed from scratch in India and spanning English and 10 Indian languages.

In a recent development, chariot is one of the first four teams selected by the mission to build sovereign foundation models. The unveiling took place at Chariot One, a launch and research showcase at Bharat Mandapam in Upcoming Delhi, bringing the government-backed programme together with a public demonstration of the lab’s speech research.

IndiaAI reports three design elements: IndicShift, a shared alphabet for Indian scripts using 2.5 times fewer tokens on Indian text; Nested Training, which develops three model sizes in a single run with 62% faster training; and Mixture of Vocabularies, an approach delivering 38% faster training.

Industry observers note that those choices address two distinct parts of multilingual development: how efficiently Indian text is represented and how much training work is required to produce different model sizes. They also indicate that Chariot-1 is intended as a reusable model family rather than only a single speech product.

Beyond text representation, the models support context-aware speech generation. IndiaAI reports more than 97% verbalization accuracy on the Async TTS Pronunciation Benchmark, which measures whether written expressions receive an acceptable spoken interpretation. That capability matters because applications must read currencies, dates, abbreviations and symbols appropriately, rather than merely pronounce individual words.

According to recent reports, the inauguration follows two public speech releases from the lab. Chariot’s November 12, 2026 release describes Chariot-1-TTS-Multilingual as generating speech in 11 Indic languages and English, with more than 50 voices, language mixing within sentences and voice cloning from a few seconds of reference audio. It also interprets prices, dates, abbreviations and symbols in context, reducing the need for custom text-normalization rules.

Industry observers note that in Chariot’s own November 11, 2026 evaluation, the model ranked first among the configurations compared on three measures: a 7.60% Hindi character error rate, 93.78% English verbalization accuracy on its English suite and a 4.901 NISQA score, an automated estimate of audio quality. Those measurements address different parts of speech generation: intelligibility, interpretation of written text and estimated sound quality.

In a recent development, the earlier Chariot-1-ASR Realtime release, dated October 22, 2026, added streaming speech recognition in 10 Indian languages and Indian English. Chariot reports that it had the lowest word error rate in every language against every streaming API and batch model tested, and that its 10-language average had 26% fewer errors than Google Gemini 3.5 Transcribe’s batch API.

Sources indicate that the release describes the system as the Chariot-1 speech-reasoning backbone post-trained for one task, rather than a model built exclusively for recognition. That makes it a public example of how the foundation model can be adapted to a specific task.

Recent findings suggest that chariot is headquartered in Delhi and led by co-founders Parth Sarthi and Suvrat Bhooshan. Its research roadmap calls for a speech-native model that reasons across meaning, delivery, timing and action, rather than dividing conversations among separate transcription, synthesis, dubbing and voice-agent pipelines. The current TTS and ASR systems are the first public steps, with developers able to generate and stream speech through the Chariot platform and API.

Recent findings suggest that the inauguration connects India’s sovereign-AI policy with a specific technical approach: build shared multilingual foundations, then adapt them to individual speech tasks. The next substantive test is whether Chariot can extend that approach from generation and recognition into the broader reasoning system it describes while retaining the efficiency and accuracy gains reported for the initial models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cachyOS, a performance-focused distribution based on Arch Linux, has announced its November 2026 release. Notable changes in this release include a upcoming recovery environment ("cachyos-recovery") for rolling back broken systems, Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) v2 support for games that require EAC to run, version 2.0.0 of the CachyOS Package Installer, and more.

1. DRM and anticheat are, to a large part, one and the same, including that they're trying to best-effort solve a theoretically impossible problem by locking down clients.

Not purchasing DRM-requiring games is really the best way to do this. Until then, refuse to help deploy such mechanisms (can't really not help with implementation unless you also think that no one should be able to do lockdown-like things to their own hardware or avoiding contributing to any such thing). Game studios certainly have the right to release games that require it. It's just better if no one buys them then.

Thankfully, there are parts of the world that do not have to live "under 17 USC 1201-1202".

If they finagle your userspace in a way you dislike, you just have to live with it.

After that came Secure Boot, which when enabled (and the security hysteria is that you must always have it enabled, even though its driving use case of "not allowing any untrusted code to run before the antivirus starts" is not very relevant for Linux) makes it harder to use a self-compiled kernel. It seems that, outside of source-focused distributions, we've grown complacent and got too comfortable letting someone else compile the software we use. Quick question: can you, with a single command, download and rebuild any package of your favorite distribution (in a way which allows easily applying local changes to it), or does it require deep developer knowlege and a bunch of esoteric commands with a long list of magic options?

There is a very big difference between downloading binaries to save time and resources and binaries being the only option available. I just created my own Linux distro and it aims to achieve two things: 1) A simple core system which can be completely understood, audited, altered, and built entirely from source by a single individual (the entire distro can be bootstrapped from a single script). 2) A package management system with online repos so that you are not required to port or compile large packages yourself. I may not always want to build Firefox, COSMIC, or the kernel myself, especially not on my older hardware. But I do want it to be possible. I do want to be able to see the code and to alter the code if I want or need to. I do want to be able to build and host it locally as well.

In a recent development, I think that is because for quite some games, a well-designed anti-cheat actually adds value. For public competitive games, cheating is a real problem, and can easily make the difference between a fun game, and a frustrating experience. This is different than with videos etc. – I don’t have any benefit from them being DRM’d vs free. The best case is, I don’t notice much difference to the unlocked video, and from there it only gets worse – so the unlocked version is always better. Recent findings suggest that in the DRM case, your computer is siding with the music/movie/media industry and against you, because it's in their interest to not allow you to make copies. No. This sounds like you're advocating for relaxing the "your computer, your rules" principle (or whatever metaphor you're using for "general purpose computing") in certain circumstances, to "play along nicely with others", or whatever. Who gets to decide how much and how often and the exact circumstances of that relaxation? Once it's out of your hands a little, it's out of your hands completely. I *still* don't care about online games (like at all), but the problem seems to be a misalignment of "where" vs. "on whose behalf" computation is performed. If the business model or design or whatever is inherently flawed, then the whole thing deserves to fail, and propping it up at everyone else's expense is a dick move (yeah, it's endemic, but that doesn't make it a good thing). And in before bluca tries to put more words in my mouth: "Cheating in online games (or anywhere else, really) makes one an arsehole" -- is a statement I completely agree with. In practice, this is functionally equivalent to saying that every multiplayer shooter should be implemented as a streaming cloud game. To clarify what that means: The game runs on a cloud server that you don't own, and you connect to it via something resembling VNC (but hopefully more responsive). If the company operating the game runs out of money or decides the game is no longer profitable, you lose access permanently. It may interest you to learn that there is an ongoing movement to get game studios to move *away* from models like this, precisely because of the ownership problem. Studios are already in the business of taking your money and then clawing back the game after a few years, even when the only thing their servers actually do is matchmaking and a little bit of cheat detection (far from enough to rule out all cases of cheating, just catching simple and obvious things like teleporting across the map or whatnot). You're suggesting that these companies restructure their software so that it is fundamentally impossible for consumers to own games, rather than merely an implementation detail specific to their current business models.

In a recent development, you have no idea what you're talking about, then. Cheating detection is not about computing somewhere else, the game server _still_ needs to run all the game state calculations. Recent changes in games like Counter-Strike even add server-side blinding so that players' computers no longer even _have_ the full gamestate. So players receive enemies' positions only milliseconds before they become visible, minimizing the impact of wallhacks. Cheaters use software to get super-human pointing, tracking, and reaction speed accuracy. And this is not something you can prevent with server-side computation.

Recent findings suggest that no, but you can make it more costly. To quote what I wrote a few comments above: > No mitigation or security measurement is perfect; it is always about making things more expensive for the attacker – expensive not only as in money, but also time and knowledge for example. And the harder it is to circumvent an anti-cheat trivially/unnoticed, the less people will cheat, and the more people will have a better game experience. And it makes a huge difference if 1/2 matches are poisoned by cheaters, or if only 1/5 games are poisoned, or even better only 1/10 games. Also, unlike with movies/DRM/data-at-rest encryption in general, cheats are usually online/active attacks and operate against a moving target – if a significant amount of players can find them online, the devs can too – and then they can detect-and-ban, or implement mitigations.

This is also why most games apply bans in waves, rather than incrementally as cheaters are detected. The goal is to catch lots of cheaters by surprise, instead of banning a couple of people and tipping your hand to the rest. (And before anyone asks: Yes, a Sybil attack is possible, but costly, because each new account requires you to buy the game again. So getting banned is a real deterrent, not just a "rotate your IP address and try again" exercise.).
